pointers.sentence: If the iterable has a `close` method, which a synchronous generator has, that method is added to the response's closers; an asynchronous generator has none, and adds nothing (`django/http/response.py:StreamingHttpResponse._set_streaming_content`).

A middleware that wants to change a streamed body cannot edit it; it assigns `streaming_content` a new iterator that wraps the old one, which is how `GZipMiddleware` compresses a stream piece by piece (`django/http/response.py:StreamingHttpResponse.streaming_content`, `django/middleware/gzip.py:GZipMiddleware.process_response`).

Code that handles responses in general is expected to look first at the class attribute `streaming`, true here and false on `HttpResponse`, and the middleware Django ships do, leaving undone what would need the body: `CommonMiddleware` adds no `Content-Length` to a streaming response, the cache middleware does not store one, and no `"ETag"` is computed for one (`django/middleware/common.py:CommonMiddleware.process_response`, `django/middleware/cache.py:UpdateCacheMiddleware.process_response`, `django/utils/cache.py:set_response_etag`).

`WSGIHandler.__call__` returns the response object and a WSGI server iterates whatever it is given: each turn of its loop asks the iterator that `StreamingHttpResponse.__iter__` returned for one more piece, which runs a synchronous generator as far as its next `yield` (`django/http/response.py:StreamingHttpResponse.__iter__`).

An exception raised there is not turned into Django's error page, since no layer of the chain is on the stack to catch it: it comes out of the iterator into the server's loop, Django logs nothing, and a server that catches it and calls `close`, as wsgiref's does, still ends the request (`django/http/response.py:StreamingHttpResponse.__iter__`).

`request_finished` is sent by the response's `close`, which the server calls after the last piece, so the request's resources are still held while the body streams (`django/http/response.py:HttpResponseBase.close`).

An ASGI handler sends the response itself, as messages: `ASGIHandler.send_response` sends the status and headers in one, and then the body, in messages of at most `ASGIHandler.chunk_size`, 65,536 bytes (`django/core/handlers/asgi.py:ASGIHandler.send_response`).

A synchronous one cannot be run on the event loop without stopping every other request while it works, so `__aiter__` warns and hands it to a thread, which runs it to its end and collects what it yields into a list; only then are the parts sent (`django/http/response.py:StreamingHttpResponse.__aiter__`).

Under ASGI that is a synchronous iterator; under WSGI it is an asynchronous one, which `StreamingHttpResponse.__iter__` runs to its end through `async_to_sync`, with the matching warning (`django/http/response.py:StreamingHttpResponse.__iter__`).

A client that leaves in the middle is noticed by the handler, which listens for a disconnection while it sends, then cancels the sending where it waits and closes the response as at the end ([The two entry points](../handlers/entry.md#an-asgi-request)) (`django/core/handlers/asgi.py:ASGIHandler.handle`).
Given anything else it behaves as its base class (`django/http/response.py:FileResponse._set_streaming_content`).

For both of these headers the name is the response's `filename` argument if one was given, and otherwise the file's own (`django/http/response.py:FileResponse.set_headers`, `django/utils/http.py:content_disposition_header`).

For both of these headers the name is the response's `filename` argument if one was given, and otherwise the file's own (`django/http/response.py:FileResponse.set_headers`, `django/utils/http.py:content_disposition_header`).

A name that Python recognises as a compressed file, such as `"report.csv.gz"`, is given the compressed file's own type, here `"application/gzip"`, and no Content-Encoding, so that a browser does not uncompress the file (`django/http/response.py:FileResponse.set_headers`).

A WSGI server that is simply given the response iterates it like any other streaming response, and gets the file a block at a time, in pieces of at most 4096 bytes (`django/http/response.py:FileResponse._set_streaming_content`).

When the response has a file and the server offers the wrapper, `WSGIHandler.__call__` replaces the file's `close` with the response's and returns, in place of the response, the server's wrapper around the file, made with the response's block size; the server sends the file by whatever means it has (`django/core/handlers/wsgi.py:WSGIHandler.__call__`).

A server that uses the wrapper calls `close` on the wrapper and not on the response, and without the replacement nothing would close the response: the request's uploaded files would stay open, and `request_finished` would never be sent (`django/core/handlers/wsgi.py:WSGIHandler.__call__`).

`ASGIHandler.run_get_response` sets the response's block size to the handler's chunk size, and the file is read to its end in a thread and held in memory before any of it is sent (`django/core/handlers/asgi.py:ASGIHandler.run_get_response`).

It calls each, ignoring any `Exception` one raises so that the rest still run, empties the list, marks the response closed, and sends `request_finished` (`django/http/response.py:HttpResponseBase.close`).

`close` is called from outside, once the body has been sent or the client has gone: by a WSGI server, by the ASGI handler after `send_response`, and by the test client, which closes an ordinary response before its call returns and a streaming one once the test has read `streaming_content` to its end ([The two entry points](../handlers/entry.md#who-ends-the-request), [The test client: `Client` and `ClientHandler`](../testing/client.md#the-servers-part-clienthandler__call)) (`django/test/client.py:ClientHandler.__call__`, `django/test/client.py:closing_iterator_wrapper`).
